promptText: What is the core idea behind Inversion of Control (IoC) in Spring, and how does Dependency Injection relate to it?
options: IoC is the general principle that object creation/wiring control is transferred to the container; DI is the specific technique Spring uses to achieve it
IoC and DI are two unrelated Spring features that happen to be taught together
DI is the general principle, and IoC is one specific way of implementing DI using @Autowired
IoC means Spring inverts the order in which HTTP request handlers execute
explanation: IoC is the principle that the framework, not application code, decides when and how dependencies are created and wired; Dependency Injection is the concrete mechanism Spring uses to realize that principle by supplying collaborators rather than letting classes construct them. The relationship runs principle-to-technique in that order, not the reverse, and neither concept has anything to do with HTTP request ordering.

promptText: A class has a constructor with seven parameters, all wired via constructor injection. A teammate suggests switching to field injection to 'clean up' the noisy constructor. What is the flaw in that suggestion?
options: Field injection would hide the same design smell instead of fixing it; the long constructor is signaling the class has too many responsibilities and should be split
Field injection is objectively superior to constructor injection in every case, so the suggestion is correct
Field injection is not possible when a class already has a constructor defined
Switching to field injection would make the class's dependencies mandatory, unlike the current constructor
explanation: A constructor with too many parameters is a visible design smell pointing at a class doing too much; switching to field injection doesn't reduce the number of dependencies, it just hides the smell by making it invisible in the source, and it also removes the ability to make fields final and easily testable. Field injection can coexist with any existing constructor, and it makes dependencies less explicit/mandatory-looking, not more.

promptText: A singleton-scoped @Service stores the current request's user ID in an instance field so a later method in the same request can read it. Under concurrent load, what specifically goes wrong, and why does 'singleton' not protect against it?
options: Multiple threads share the one singleton instance, so concurrent requests can overwrite each other's instance-field value; 'singleton' only guarantees one shared instance, not safe concurrent access to it
Nothing goes wrong, because Spring automatically synchronizes access to every singleton bean's fields
The bean will throw an exception on the second concurrent request because Spring detects the shared mutable field
Singleton beans are recreated per request, so each request already gets a fresh instance field with no risk
explanation: Because a singleton is one shared instance across all threads, storing per-request state in an instance field lets concurrent requests race on that same field, corrupting or leaking data between users; Spring provides no automatic synchronization or per-request isolation for singleton fields. Singleton beans are created once at startup (not per request), which is exactly why request-specific data belongs in method parameters/local variables instead.

promptText: Which stereotype annotation adds real extra runtime behavior beyond simply registering a bean via component scanning?
options: @Repository, which enables translation of database exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy
@Component, which enables AOP proxying for every bean it annotates
@Service, which automatically wraps every method in a transaction
@Controller, which enables constructor injection specifically for web-layer beans
explanation: @Repository is meta-annotated with @Component like the others, but it additionally activates a BeanPostProcessor that translates vendor-specific persistence exceptions into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy. @Service does not automatically add transactions (that still requires @Transactional), and neither @Component nor @Controller add AOP proxying or constructor-injection behavior on their own -- they differ from @Component mostly in semantic intent.

promptText: Why does ApplicationContext eagerly creating singleton beans at startup count as a practical advantage over BeanFactory's lazy instantiation, rather than just being wasted startup time?
options: Configuration and wiring errors surface immediately at startup (fail fast) instead of appearing later, mid-request, in production
Eager creation reduces the application's memory footprint compared to lazy loading
Eager creation is required for Spring AOP proxies to be created at all
Eager creation guarantees thread-safe access to every bean once the context finishes starting
explanation: Because ApplicationContext eagerly instantiates singletons at startup, misconfiguration or missing dependencies cause a startup failure rather than an error deep into a production request -- a deliberate fail-fast trade-off, not primarily a memory optimization. AOP proxies can be created regardless of eager/lazy singleton timing, and eager creation says nothing about thread-safety of bean state once running.

promptText: UserService depends on OrderService via constructor injection, and OrderService depends on UserService via constructor injection, forming a cycle. A developer wonders why switching both to field injection would let the app start, while constructor injection fails outright. What explains the difference?
options: Constructor injection requires both objects fully built before either constructor can run, which is impossible in a cycle; field injection can construct each bean with a no-arg-like step first and inject the (possibly still-initializing) fields afterward
Field injection and constructor injection behave identically for circular dependencies; the app would fail to start either way
Constructor injection fails only because Spring cannot use CGLIB proxies on constructor parameters
The cycle is only a problem if the beans are prototype-scoped; singleton beans never have this issue regardless of injection style
explanation: Constructor injection needs each dependency fully constructed and passed in before the constructor body can even run, which is fundamentally unsatisfiable in a two-way cycle, causing a BeanCurrentlyInCreationException; field/setter injection instantiates each bean first (via its own default construction path) and only afterward reaches in via reflection to set fields, so a partially-built reference can be injected. This has nothing to do with CGLIB proxying, and the cycle problem applies to singleton beans specifically (not something avoided by scope).

promptText: In Spring AOP terminology, what specifically distinguishes a 'pointcut' from a 'join point'?
options: A join point is a candidate point in execution (always a method execution in Spring AOP); a pointcut is the expression that selects which join points the advice actually applies to
A join point and a pointcut are two names for the exact same concept, used interchangeably
A pointcut is the code that actually runs when triggered, while a join point is the module packaging the concern
A join point can only exist inside a pointcut expression, never independently
explanation: A join point is a potential point where advice could apply (in Spring AOP, always a method execution), while a pointcut is the expression (e.g., 'all methods in the service package') that selects which of those join points the advice targets -- they are distinct, related concepts, not synonyms. The code that runs is the advice, and the module packaging the concern is the aspect, so neither term matches 'pointcut' or 'join point' in this question.

promptText: A caching aspect is written using @Before advice so it can check the cache before the method executes and skip calling the real method entirely on a cache hit. Why won't this actually work as intended?
options: @Before cannot prevent the target method from executing at all; only @Around, via its ProceedingJoinPoint, can choose not to call proceed() and short-circuit the invocation
@Before advice runs after the target method completes, so it is too late to check the cache beforehand
@Before advice can only be applied to constructors, never to regular methods
The caching aspect will work exactly as intended; @Before is fully capable of skipping the target method
explanation: @Before advice runs before the method but has no mechanism to stop the method from subsequently executing -- only @Around, which receives a ProceedingJoinPoint and controls whether/when proceed() is called, can short-circuit the invocation entirely (exactly how a real caching aspect returns a cached value without invoking the target). @Before runs before, not after, the target method, and it applies to ordinary methods just fine -- the problem is specifically its lack of control over whether the method runs.

promptText: A Spring-managed bean's target class implements no interfaces. Which proxy mechanism does Spring AOP use to advise it, and what does that choice restrict about the class's methods?
options: CGLIB, which subclasses the target class at runtime, meaning the class and its advised methods cannot be final
JDK dynamic proxy, since it works for any class regardless of whether interfaces are present
Spring cannot proxy the bean at all in this case, so no AOP advice will ever apply
A hand-written wrapper class that the developer must generate manually at compile time
explanation: When no interface is present, Spring falls back to CGLIB, which subclasses the concrete class at runtime and overrides its methods to insert advice -- since overriding is the mechanism, the target class and its advised methods cannot be final or private. JDK dynamic proxies specifically require the target to implement an interface, so they are not usable here, and Spring does not require any manually-written wrapper class.

promptText: A @Transactional method is marked `final` on a bean with no interfaces (so CGLIB proxying applies). Separately, a colleague says the fix is to switch to JDK dynamic proxies instead, since 'JDK proxies can handle final methods.' Evaluate this claim.
options: The claim is wrong on two counts: JDK proxies require an interface (which this bean lacks), and even if one existed, the underlying problem -- CGLIB subclassing cannot override final methods -- is unrelated to which proxy type is chosen once CGLIB is in play
The claim is correct; switching to JDK dynamic proxies is a valid, standard fix for final methods on interface-less beans
Final methods are never a problem for either proxy type; the transaction failure must have an unrelated cause
JDK dynamic proxies also use subclassing internally, so they share the exact same final-method restriction as CGLIB
explanation: JDK dynamic proxies require the target to implement an interface, which this bean does not have, so switching to them isn't even an option here; the real fix is removing the final modifier so CGLIB can override the method. JDK proxies work by implementing an interface, not by subclassing, so they don't share CGLIB's final-method restriction in the abstract, but that's moot since they can't be used on an interface-less bean at all.

promptText: Inside UserService, methodA() calls this.methodB() directly, where methodB() is annotated @Transactional. A developer 'fixes' this by adding @Transactional to methodA() as well, expecting methodB()'s annotation to now take effect through the outer transaction. Does this work, and why?
options: It works, but not for the reason assumed: methodA()'s own @Transactional now creates the proxy-mediated transaction, and methodB() simply runs inside it via REQUIRED propagation joining the same transaction -- methodB()'s own annotation is still bypassed by the internal call
It does not work at all, because self-invocation permanently disables @Transactional for the rest of that bean's lifetime
It works because Spring detects the internal call and automatically re-routes it through the proxy once methodA() is also transactional
It works only because methodB() was called via this, which Spring treats as equivalent to calling it through the proxy
explanation: Annotating methodA() as @Transactional means calls to methodA() now go through the proxy and start a real transaction; methodB(), called via 'this' from inside methodA(), still bypasses its own proxy-mediated advice, but since it executes within methodA()'s already-active transaction (default REQUIRED propagation), it ends up transactional anyway -- just not because its own @Transactional annotation did anything. Spring does not detect or re-route internal calls, and self-invocation doesn't permanently disable anything; it's a per-call bypass of the proxy, not a switch that gets flipped.

promptText: Which transaction propagation setting should be used for an audit-log write that must persist even if the surrounding business transaction later rolls back, and why won't REQUIRED work for this case?
options: REQUIRES_NEW, because it suspends the current transaction and starts an independent one that commits or rolls back on its own; REQUIRED would join the same transaction, so an outer rollback would also roll back the audit write
REQUIRED, because it always creates a brand-new transaction for every method call regardless of an existing one
MANDATORY, because it guarantees the audit write commits independently of any caller's transaction state
NEVER, because it forces the audit write to run outside of any transactional context entirely, which guarantees durability
explanation: REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and starts a new, independent one that commits or rolls back on its own, which is exactly why it's used for audit logging that must survive an outer rollback. REQUIRED joins the existing transaction rather than creating a new one every time, so an outer rollback would also roll back the audit write; MANDATORY only joins an existing transaction (throwing if none exists) and NEVER forbids running with a transaction at all, so neither provides the independent-commit guarantee needed here.

promptText: Transaction A reads a row at READ_COMMITTED isolation, then Transaction B updates and commits that same row, and when A reads the row again in the same transaction, it sees B's new value. Which anomaly is this, and which isolation level would have prevented it?
options: Non-repeatable read; REPEATABLE_READ (or stronger) would have prevented it by keeping any row read within a transaction stable for its duration
Dirty read; READ_COMMITTED itself should have already prevented this, so the scenario is impossible as described
Phantom read; only SERIALIZABLE could have prevented it since new rows are involved
Lost update; using pessimistic locking on the initial read is the only way to prevent this specific anomaly
explanation: A non-repeatable read occurs when the same row's value differs across two reads within one transaction because another transaction committed a change in between; READ_COMMITTED only guarantees you never read uncommitted data, not that data stays stable across repeated reads, so REPEATABLE_READ or SERIALIZABLE is needed to prevent it. A dirty read involves seeing uncommitted data (not what happened here, since B's write was committed), and a phantom read specifically concerns new/disappearing rows in a repeated query's result set, not a changed value in an existing row.

promptText: What is the role of a BeanPostProcessor in Spring's bean creation flow, and which Spring feature relies on it?
options: It provides before/after initialization hooks invoked for every bean; AOP and transaction support use it to wrap beans in proxies after they're initialized
It scans packages to discover classes annotated with stereotype annotations before any bean definitions exist
It defines how many instances of a bean the container creates, i.e., the bean's scope
It manages the lifecycle of database connections used by @Transactional methods
explanation: BeanPostProcessor exposes before/after initialization callbacks invoked for every bean, which is the exact mechanism AOP and transaction support use to wrap beans in proxies, and which annotation-driven injection (@Autowired, @Value) relies on as well. Component scanning (package discovery) and bean scope are separate, earlier-stage container concerns, and connection lifecycle management is handled by the transaction manager, not BeanPostProcessor.

promptText: A method annotated @Transactional throws a checked (non-RuntimeException) exception that propagates out of the method. By default, does Spring roll back the transaction?
options: No -- by default Spring only rolls back on unchecked (runtime) exceptions and errors, unless rollbackFor is explicitly configured
Yes -- Spring always rolls back on any exception, checked or unchecked, with no configuration needed
No -- @Transactional never triggers a rollback under any circumstances, regardless of exception type
Yes -- but only because checked exceptions are automatically wrapped into RuntimeException before being rethrown
explanation: Spring's default rollback rule only covers unchecked exceptions and errors; a checked exception propagating out of a @Transactional method still commits unless rollbackFor is explicitly configured, a common source of unexpected commits when checked exceptions are used for error signaling. Spring does not automatically wrap checked exceptions into RuntimeException before deciding whether to roll back -- the checked/unchecked distinction is exactly what the default rule keys on.
